Chapter 11: The Broader Consequences—Population, Environment, and the Future
When you think about bringing a new person into the world, it might seem like a private, personal choice—maybe even a philosophical debate. But there’s something bigger at play here. This decision ripples out, touching society, the environment, and the future of our entire planet.
Picture a city that’s growing faster every year. The streets are packed, resources are running low, and you can feel the pressure everywhere—from crowded schools to polluted air. As more people arrive, the planet feels the strain: more pollution, more habitats lost, and climate change picking up speed. Choosing to have a child isn’t just a family matter. It shapes the world we all call home.
Most of us want to leave something better behind. We hope our children will thrive, that the world will become safer and kinder. But here’s something to pay attention to—every new life, no matter how loved, adds a little more pressure to our already fragile planet. And as more people are born, the chances of suffering grow right along with the population.
The harm that can come with existence isn’t just a private burden. It’s something we all share—a collective challenge that stretches far beyond one family, or even one generation. Whenever someone decides to have a child, it affects not just that child, but the world they’ll inherit.
Some people believe the answer lies in making society better—fighting for less suffering, and creating more opportunities for everyone. That’s a worthy goal. But even if we succeed, the reality remains: every new life faces risks. We can’t wipe out every danger; we can only try to manage them.
And as our city grows, those challenges become impossible to ignore. Suddenly, the question of having children isn’t just about personal dreams or hopes—it’s a global concern. The harm of coming into existence isn’t simply a matter of choice. It’s something that affects us all.
When we step back and look at the bigger picture, it changes the way we think about the value of existence. It’s not enough to just hope for a brighter future, or to assume life is always a gift. The risks and the hardships are real. And facing them—honestly, together—is something we owe ourselves, and the generations yet to come.
